edit.text: Do not blanket-forbid cuts after nouns or their specifiers. Ask instead: would forbidding this noun+modifier cut force other cuts into very-short pieces (about ≤3–5 words) that split subject–verb, verb–object, or internal compounds? If so, allow the noun+modifier cut; otherwise avoid it.

findings.diagnosis: The prompt underestimates the contradiction risk of leaving trailing adjuncts/ modifiers as standalone pieces (participial, prepositional, 'using...' phrases, 'in advance', 'and beyond'). Such trailing fragments often cannot be interpreted correctly on their own and create high contra when separated.
findings.evidence: ['en_us_845','en_us_1081','en_us_738','en_us_396']: in each case the policy left a trailing adjunct or participial/prepositional fragment alone (e.g. 'using spray paint', 'and beyond', 'more than one month', 'invasion routes as the'), producing high contra or a contra_kill; the target re-attached those modifiers and regained cohesion.

edit.text: Treat cuts that leave only postverbal or postnominal adjuncts (prepositional, participial, 'using...' phrases, 'in advance', 'and beyond') as high-contradiction risk unless the fragment can stand as an independent proposition; prefer keeping such modifiers attached to their heads.

findings.diagnosis: The prompt lacks short, concrete examples showing when to allow a noun+modifier cut to prevent worse subject‑verb fragmentation; scorers need a model example that trades a noun+modifier split for preserving a subject or predicate in very-short bins.
